analogy.p: Imagine sorting a pile of exam papers by mark. Bubble sort is like standing in a line of students and asking neighbours to swap places whenever the one on the left has a higher number than the one on the right, over and over until nobody swaps. Insertion sort is like picking up papers one at a time and sliding each into the right place in the stack already in your hand. Merge sort is like splitting the pile among many friends, each sorting a tiny pile, then pairs of friends merging their piles by always taking the lower mark from the top of either pile. The analogy breaks down because a computer can only compare two values at a time and cannot 'glance' at the whole pile to see which is lowest.
analogy.t: Sorting a pile of exam papers

bullets: Sorting means rearranging the **same items** into order; no items are added or lost, only their positions change.

Numbers are compared by value (2 comes before 10); text is compared character by character using **character codes** (so 'Apple' sorts before 'apple' in some systems because capital letters have lower codes).

The three algorithms differ in **method**: bubble sort swaps neighbours, insertion sort builds a sorted section by inserting one item at a time, merge sort **divides** the list and **merges** sorted halves.
They also differ in **efficiency**: how many comparisons and moves are needed, and how much extra memory is used.
Every sorting algorithm needs two basic operations: **compare** two items and **move or swap** items.
Link to other topics: sorting prepares data for **binary search** (2.1.3), and sorting is built from **iteration**, **selection** and **arrays** (2.2).
Exam questions are of two types: **trace** an algorithm on given data, or **explain/compare** the algorithms in words.
core.h: What a sorting algorithm is and why we need one
core.p: A **sorting algorithm** is a set of step-by-step instructions that takes a list of items and puts them into a stated order, usually **ascending** (smallest to largest, or A to Z) or **descending** (largest to smallest, or Z to A). The OCR J277 specification (section 2.1.3) requires you to know three **standard sorting algorithms**: **bubble sort**, **insertion sort** and **merge sort**. You must be able to explain how each works, trace each one on a short list of data, and compare them. Sorting matters because sorted data is far easier to use: a sorted list can be searched with the much faster **binary search**, duplicates sit next to each other, and people find sorted results easier to read.

bullets: In each pass, compare item 1 with item 2, then item 2 with item 3, then item 3 with item 4, and so on to the end of the list.
If the left item is **greater than** the right item (for ascending order), **swap** them; otherwise leave them.
After pass 1 the **largest** value is guaranteed to be at the end. After pass 2 the second largest is in place, and so on.
Because the end of the list is already correct after each pass, later passes can stop one position earlier (an optimisation).
A **swapped flag** (a Boolean variable) records whether any swap happened in a pass. If it is still False at the end, the list is sorted and the algorithm stops.
A list of n items needs at most **n - 1** passes to be sorted, even without the flag.
A swap needs a **temporary variable**: temp = a, a = b, b = temp. Without it one value would be overwritten and lost.
core.p: **Bubble sort** repeatedly steps through the list, comparing each pair of **adjacent** (neighbouring) items and **swapping** them if they are in the wrong order. One full run through the list is called a **pass**. During a pass, the largest value that has not yet been placed 'bubbles up' to the end of the list, like a bubble rising through water. Passes are repeated until a complete pass is made with **no swaps**, which proves the list is sorted. It is the simplest of the three algorithms to understand and write, but it is slow on large lists because it makes so many comparisons.

bullets: **Pass 2:** compare 3,5 (no swap); 5,1 (swap) gives [3,1,5,4,8]; 5,4 (swap) gives [3,1,4,5,8]. The comparison of 5 with 8 is not needed because 8 is already in place. Swaps: 2.
**Pass 3:** compare 3,1 (swap) gives [1,3,4,5,8]; 3,4 (no swap); 4,5 (no swap). Swaps: 1.
**Pass 4:** compare 1,3; 3,4; 4,5; no swaps at all, so the flag stays False and the algorithm **stops**. The sorted list is [1,3,4,5,8].
Notice that the list became sorted during pass 3, but the algorithm only **knows** this after pass 4 made no swaps. A final check pass is always needed.
Small values (like 1) move **left only one place per pass**, whereas large values can move right many places in one pass. This is why bubble sort is slow when small values start near the end.
In a trace question, write a new row or line for every pass, and circle or underline the pair being compared if the question asks for each comparison.
core.p: Tracing means following the algorithm exactly and writing down the list after each comparison or pass. Take the list [5, 3, 8, 1, 4] sorted into ascending order. In pass 1: compare 5 and 3, 5 is bigger so swap, giving [3, 5, 8, 1, 4]. Compare 5 and 8, already in order, no swap. Compare 8 and 1, swap, giving [3, 5, 1, 8, 4]. Compare 8 and 4, swap, giving [3, 5, 1, 4, 8]. The largest value, 8, is now at the end. Pass 1 made three swaps. Always show every pass clearly because mark schemes award a mark for each correct intermediate list.

bullets: swapped = true at the start makes sure the **while loop runs at least once**; it is set back to false at the start of every pass.
The **inner for loop** goes to n - 2 (with a zero-indexed array) so that a[i+1] never goes past the last element; going one too far gives an **index out of range** error.
The comparison operator decides the order: > gives **ascending** order, < gives **descending** order. Changing it is a common exam question.
**Best case:** a list that is already sorted needs just **one pass** (n - 1 comparisons, no swaps) if a flag is used.
**Worst case:** a list in reverse order needs the most passes and swaps, since every pair is wrong at the start.

Number of comparisons grows roughly with the **square** of the list size, so doubling the list size about **quadruples** the work. (Big-O notation O(n squared) is beyond the OCR GCSE specification but helps you understand why bubble sort is slow.)
Bubble sort uses **no extra memory** apart from a temporary variable: it sorts the list 'in place'.
**Advantages:** simple, short code, easy to trace, no extra memory. **Disadvantage:** inefficient for large lists.
core.h: Bubble sort: pseudocode, flag and efficiency
core.p: In exams you may be asked to **complete**, **read** or **explain** bubble sort pseudocode. The OCR style uses for loops and a while loop controlled by the swapped flag. The outer while loop repeats whole passes; the inner for loop does one pass; the selection statement decides whether to swap. A common version is: swapped = true; while swapped == true; swapped = false; for i = 0 to n - 2; if a[i] > a[i+1] then temp = a[i]; a[i] = a[i+1]; a[i+1] = temp; swapped = true; endif; next i; endwhile. Understanding what each line is for earns more marks than memorising the code.

bullets: At the start, the first item on its own counts as a **sorted section of length one**.
Take the next item (the **key**) and compare it with the items in the sorted section, working from the **right-hand end** leftwards.
While an item in the sorted section is **greater than** the key, shift that item one place **right** to make a gap.
When you reach an item that is not greater than the key (or reach the start of the list), **drop the key into the gap**.
Repeat for each remaining item. The list is sorted when the unsorted section is empty.
Unlike bubble sort, items are **not repeatedly swapped**; they are shifted and each key is placed once.
The key must be **stored in a variable** before shifting begins, otherwise it would be overwritten by the shift.
core.p: **Insertion sort** works by splitting the list into a **sorted section** (at the start) and an **unsorted section** (the rest). It takes the first item of the unsorted section, called the **key**, and **inserts** it into the correct position within the sorted section by shifting larger items one place to the right. This is exactly how many people sort a hand of playing cards: pick up one card at a time and slide it into the right place among the cards already in your hand. The sorted section grows by one item each time until the whole list is sorted.

bullets: **After key 3:** [3, 5 | 8, 1, 4]. One shift (the 5). The bar | separates sorted from unsorted.
**After key 8:** [3, 5, 8 | 1, 4]. **Zero shifts**, because 8 is already larger than everything before it.
**After key 1:** [1, 3, 5, 8 | 4]. Three shifts, since 1 is smaller than all the sorted items.
**After key 4:** [1, 3, 4, 5, 8]. Two shifts. The list is sorted.
If the list is **already sorted**, no shifting is ever needed, so insertion sort is very fast on **nearly sorted** data.
If the list is in **reverse order**, every key must be shifted all the way to the front, which is the worst case.
A tracing mistake to avoid: do not move the key to the right place by swapping with the whole list; work only inside the **sorted section**.
core.p: Take the list [5, 3, 8, 1, 4]. Start with sorted section [5] and unsorted section [3, 8, 1, 4]. Key = 3: 5 is greater than 3 so shift 5 right and insert 3 at the front, giving sorted section [3, 5]. Key = 8: 5 is not greater than 8, so 8 stays where it is: [3, 5, 8]. Key = 1: shift 8, then 5, then 3 to the right and put 1 at the start: [1, 3, 5, 8]. Key = 4: shift 8 and 5 right, but 3 is not greater than 4, so insert 4 after 3: [1, 3, 4, 5, 8]. Each line of working shows the sorted section growing, which is what examiners look for.

bullets: The inner loop condition has **two parts** joined by AND: stay inside the list (j >= 0) and the item is still bigger than the key. If either is false the loop stops.
a[j+1] = a[j] is a **shift** (copy to the right), not a swap, so it needs no temporary variable apart from the stored key.
Insertion sort sorts **in place**, using almost no extra memory, like bubble sort.
It is **more efficient than bubble sort** on most data because it moves each item once into position, and it can stop comparing early.
It is good for **small lists** and for lists that are **nearly sorted**, for example adding a few new records to an already sorted file.
For large random lists it is still slow compared with merge sort, because many items are shifted many places.
Exam trap: the sorted section is at the **left**, but the comparisons start at its **right-hand end**.
core.p: The pseudocode uses an outer loop over each key and an inner while loop that shifts items. For i = 1 to n - 1: key = a[i]; j = i - 1; while j >= 0 AND a[j] > key; a[j+1] = a[j]; j = j - 1; endwhile; a[j+1] = key; next i. The outer loop starts at index 1 because index 0 is already a sorted section of one. The inner loop shifts bigger items right and stops when it finds a smaller item or reaches the front. After the loop, the key is written into the gap at position j + 1.

bullets: **Divide stage:** keep halving each sub-list (if the length is odd, one half has one more item) until every sub-list has exactly one item.
A list of 8 items is halved 3 times (8 to 4 to 2 to 1). A list of n items needs about **log2 n** splitting levels.
**Conquer stage:** a one-item list is sorted already, so no sorting work happens during the split.
**Combine stage:** repeatedly **merge** two sorted sub-lists into one sorted list.
The method is often written using **recursion** (a subroutine that calls itself); you do not need to write the recursive code at GCSE but you should recognise the idea.
Merge sort does the same amount of splitting and merging **whatever the original order** of the data.
Extra memory is needed because merging creates **new lists** rather than rearranging inside the old one.
core.p: **Merge sort** uses a **divide and conquer** approach: break the problem into smaller problems, solve each, then combine the results. It first **splits** the list into halves again and again until every sub-list contains **one item**. A list of one item is already sorted by definition. It then **merges** pairs of sorted sub-lists, repeatedly, into larger sorted lists until a single sorted list remains. Merge sort is much more efficient than bubble or insertion sort on large lists, but it is harder to understand and uses extra memory to hold the sub-lists.

bullets: Only the **front items** of the two lists are ever compared.
The smaller item is copied and its pointer moves on; the other pointer stays put.
When one list runs out, the rest of the other list is copied across **without further comparison**, because it is already in order.
If the two items being compared are equal, take either (usually the left-hand one first, which keeps equal items in their original order).
Merging two lists with a total of n items needs at most **n - 1** comparisons, which is quick.
A frequent error is to merge by simply joining the lists end to end (concatenation). **That does not sort**; items must be compared and interleaved.
Mark scheme language: 'compares the first items of each list', 'adds the smaller to the new list', 'repeats until one list is empty', 'adds the remaining items'.
core.h: Merge sort: how the merge step works
core.p: The key skill is the **merge** itself: combining two sorted lists into one sorted list. Place a pointer at the front of each list. Compare the two items being pointed at, copy the **smaller** one into the new list, and move that list's pointer forward by one. Repeat until one list is used up, then copy all the remaining items from the other list to the end of the new list. Because each list is already sorted, the smallest remaining item is always at one of the two fronts, so you never need to look further. For example, merging [3, 5] and [1, 8]: compare 3 and 1, take 1; compare 3 and 8, take 3; compare 5 and 8, take 5; the first list is empty, so copy 8. Result: [1, 3, 5, 8].

bullets: **Split levels:** 8 items, then two lists of 4, then four lists of 2, then eight lists of 1 (three splits).
**First merge level:** pairs of single items are merged into sorted pairs: [5]+[3] gives [3,5]; [8]+[1] gives [1,8]; [4]+[7] gives [4,7]; [2]+[6] gives [2,6].
**Final merge:** the two sorted halves become the complete sorted list.
In an exam, label the diagram 'split' going down and 'merge' coming back up, and write the sub-lists in brackets.
If a list has an odd length, for example 5 items, split into 2 and 3, then 3 splits into 1 and 2; the method is unchanged.
Sorted result is identical for all three algorithms: they differ only in **method and efficiency**, not in the answer.
core.p: Take [5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 7, 2, 6]. Split into [5,3,8,1] and [4,7,2,6]. Split again into [5,3], [8,1], [4,7], [2,6]. Split again into eight single items. Now merge in pairs: [3,5], [1,8], [4,7], [2,6]. Merge again: [3,5] with [1,8] gives [1,3,5,8]; [4,7] with [2,6] gives [2,4,6,7]. Final merge: compare 1 and 2, take 1; compare 3 and 2, take 2; compare 3 and 4, take 3; compare 5 and 4, take 4; compare 5 and 6, take 5; compare 8 and 6, take 6; compare 8 and 7, take 7; the second list is empty so copy 8. Result: [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]. Draw the split lines then the merge lines as a tree: that layout earns the method marks.

bullets: **Bubble sort:** simple to write and trace; very slow on large lists; in-place; ends early on an already sorted list (with a flag).
**Insertion sort:** simple; in-place; **faster than bubble sort** on typical data; excellent on small or nearly sorted lists; slow on large random lists.
**Merge sort:** fastest of the three on **large lists**; same performance whatever the starting order; **needs more memory**; more complex to code.
For **100 000 records** choose merge sort because the number of comparisons grows much more slowly.
For **ten items** the difference is tiny, so the simpler bubble or insertion sort is perfectly suitable.
For a list that gets **one new item at a time** and must stay sorted, insertion is a natural choice.
When memory is **very limited** (for example, a tiny embedded device), prefer an in-place algorithm over merge sort.
Use comparative words: 'faster', 'fewer comparisons', 'uses less memory', 'more complex'.
core.p: Exam questions often ask which algorithm is most suitable or why one is better than another. The answer always depends on the **size** and **order** of the data and on the **memory** available. Bubble sort and insertion sort are simple and use almost no extra memory, so they are fine for small lists. Merge sort is much faster for big lists because it avoids the huge number of comparisons the others need, but its code is longer and it needs additional memory for the sub-lists. Always make a judgement and justify it with a reason tied to the scenario.

bullets: Linear search works on any list; binary search needs a **sorted** list. Sorting first costs time, so it only pays off if you search **many times**.
Sorting uses a **for loop** (known number of passes or keys) and a **while loop** (repeat until swapped is false or position found).
Swapping needs a **temporary variable**, an everyday idea: to swap the contents of two cups you need a third empty cup.
Arrays hold the data: a[i] and a[i+1] are neighbours. The loop limit must stop at the **last valid index** to avoid an index error.
String data sorts using character codes, so 'Zebra' comes before 'apple' in a plain code comparison; this is why care is needed with case.
Sorting records in a file (for example, by surname) uses the same algorithms with one **field** used as the sort key.
Link to other topics: **trace tables** (2.1) are used to follow these algorithms, and **testing** (2.3) checks a sort works for sorted, reversed and duplicate data.
core.h: Sorting links: searching, arrays and programming
core.p: Sorting is closely tied to other parts of Paper 2. A **binary search** only works on a **sorted** list, so a program may sort first and then search. Sorting algorithms also operate on **arrays**, so you must be comfortable with indexes, loops and swapping. When writing or completing code, remember that array indexes usually start at 0 in OCR reference language. Understanding sorting also supports **computational thinking**: decomposing the problem (compare, swap, repeat), recognising patterns (the same steps repeated each pass) and using abstraction (only the order matters, not what the data means).

bullets: Trace questions: write the **full list every time**, not just the changed values, and number your passes.
If the question says 'after the first pass' give the list at the **end of pass 1 only**.

Describe questions: use the keywords **compare, adjacent, swap, pass, repeat until no swaps** for bubble sort; **sorted section, key, insert, shift** for insertion; **divide, halves, single item, merge, smaller first** for merge.
Do not describe a different algorithm: for bubble sort, never say 'find the smallest and put it first' (that is selection sort, not on the spec).
Check your answer: the final list must contain **exactly the same values** as the start, with the same number of items.
For a 'which is more efficient' question, give the algorithm **and a reason**: one mark for the choice, one for the justification.
Test your trace with a different method: count how many items are in each sub-list and check the totals.
Be ready for **descending** order; simply swap which item must be larger.
core.p: Sorting questions fall into four types. **Trace**: show the list after each pass or step. **Describe/explain**: write the method in the correct order using technical vocabulary. **Complete/fix pseudocode**: fill in a missing line such as the swap or the comparison. **Compare/choose**: justify the best algorithm for a scenario. For all of them, read the question for the required order (ascending or descending) and the number of passes asked for, because many marks are lost by stopping at the wrong point or sorting the wrong way round.

exam: **Command words:** 'State' (1 mark): name the algorithm or a fact. 'Describe' (2 to 4 marks): give the steps in order. 'Explain' (2 to 3 marks): give a point plus a reason using 'because'. 'Trace' or 'show' (2 to 4 marks): show the list at each step. 'Compare'/'discuss' (4 to 6 marks): both algorithms and a conclusion.
**1 mark:** a single fact, for example 'Merge sort splits the list into halves' or 'Bubble sort swaps adjacent items if they are in the wrong order'.
**2 marks, describe bubble sort:** 'Compare each pair of adjacent items and swap them if they are in the wrong order (1). Repeat passes through the list until no swaps are made (1).'

**3 to 4 marks, describe insertion sort:** sorted section, take next item (key), compare with items in sorted section and shift larger items right, insert the key into the gap, repeat until all items are inserted.
**3 to 4 marks, describe merge sort:** repeatedly split in half until single items, merge pairs of lists by comparing first items and taking the smaller, repeat until one sorted list.
**Trace marks** are awarded for each correct pass or merge level; wrong early values are carried forward ('follow through') so keep working.
**6-mark discuss questions:** write a paragraph on each algorithm's method and efficiency, link to the scenario (list size, memory) and end with a conclusion that names the best choice.
**Pseudocode questions:** if asked to complete the swap, remember the three lines using temp; if asked about a loop limit, think about the last index.
**Efficiency vocabulary:** 'fewer comparisons', 'more comparisons', 'extra memory', 'in place', 'large data set', 'nearly sorted'.
**Check:** after any trace, the final list must have the same number of items and the same values as the start.

mistakes.r: After one pass only the largest value is guaranteed to be in its final place at the end; more passes are needed until a pass has no swaps.
mistakes.w: Bubble sort: after the first pass the whole list is sorted.

mistakes.r: The algorithm only stops when a complete pass is made with no swaps (swapped flag is false).
mistakes.w: Stopping bubble sort as soon as the list looks sorted.

mistakes.r: A temporary variable is needed: temp = a, a = b, b = temp, otherwise the first value is overwritten and lost.
mistakes.w: Swapping by writing a = b then b = a.

mistakes.r: Larger items in the sorted section are shifted one place right and the key is inserted once into the gap.
mistakes.w: Insertion sort: swapping the key with every item.

mistakes.r: Merge sort compares the first items of each sorted sub-list and adds the smaller to a new list, repeating until all are merged.
mistakes.w: Merge sort: splitting the list and just joining the halves back together.

mistakes.r: The list is split until every sub-list contains one item, then merged back in pairs.
mistakes.w: Merge sort: splitting into two halves and sorting each half only.

mistakes.r: Merge sort uses far fewer comparisons on large lists, but it needs extra memory; mention both when comparing.
mistakes.w: Saying merge sort is better 'because it is quicker' with no detail.

mistakes.r: Bubble sort compares adjacent pairs and swaps them if out of order.
mistakes.w: Describing selection sort ('find the smallest') for bubble sort.

mistakes.r: Read the order in the question; for descending order, swap when the left item is smaller than the right.
mistakes.w: Using the wrong order (ascending when descending was asked).

summary: OCR J277 section 2.1.3 requires you to know how the bubble sort, insertion sort and merge sort algorithms work, to trace each one on a small list, and to compare them. It matters because Paper 2 regularly asks you to trace a sort, describe it using the correct keywords, or justify which sort suits a scenario.

worked.ans: Bubble sort compares adjacent records and swaps them, repeating passes until no swaps are made. With 200 000 records it would need a huge number of passes and comparisons, so it would be very slow. Merge sort repeatedly splits the list into halves until each sub-list has one record, then merges the sorted sub-lists by comparing first items and taking the smaller. It uses far fewer comparisons on a large list, so it is much faster. Its disadvantages are that it needs extra memory for the sub-lists and the code is more complex. Because the data set is large, the company should use a merge sort.

Weigh up: merge sort needs extra memory and is more complex, bubble sort is simple and uses no extra memory.
